records.name_note: All admissible sources consulted (NC State Extension, Clemson HGIC, Penn State Extension, UMD Extension, RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden) use Allium cepa as the current binomial for onion. No synonym or accepted-name discrepancy was found, so scientific_name_accepted matches scientific_name_given.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's plant database flags onion as a "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses," rating poison severity as Low, with toxic principle N-propyl disulfide, and symptoms "Vomiting, breakdown of red blood cells (hemolytic anemia, Heinz body anemia), blood in urine, weakness, high heart rate, panting." This is separate from the bulb/tops being an edible human food crop, which the same page also states.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives numeric day/night temperature values; onion is only described qualitatively as a 'cool-season crop' (Penn State, UMD).

chill_damage_f: no source states an actionable frost-damage-onset temperature. UMD Extension says onion is 'Hardy (can withstand heavy spring frosts)' but that is a mature-plant survival/tolerance statement, not a damage-onset number, so it was not used for this field.

water_regime: sources conflict. Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder rates onion's water need as 'Dry to medium,' while Clemson HGIC ('make sure onions have plenty of moisture, especially after bulbs begin enlarging') and UMD Extension ('Ensure ample moisture, especially after bulbs begin enlarging') both call for consistently ample moisture during bulb development. Left null rather than resolving the conflict.
water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering-frequency-in-days figure for onion.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source; these are outdoor garden extension pages with no ambient-humidity targets given.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good: not applicable/stated — admissible sources describe onion sun exposure only in duration terms (full sun / hours-per-day: NC State, Clemson, UMD, RHS), never as footcandle intensity, per the outdoor-crop convention.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength, fertilize_active_months: Clemson describes a three-stage fertilizer program (pre-plant broadcast of 10-10-10, sidedress with 5-10-10 plus sulfur 1-2 weeks after bulb enlargement begins, then a further sidedress with calcium nitrate about 30 days later) rather than a fixed recurring interval, a liquid-dilution strength, or a list of active months, so it wasn't mapped onto these fields.
cool_rest_note: not addressed for this outdoor annual/biennial vegetable crop by any admissible source.
soil_drainage was mapped to the catalog's 'moderate' category by interpreting repeated 'well-drained' language (Clemson, NC State, RHS); no source uses the catalog's own drainage vocabulary directly.

soil_base — removed on audit: The cited quote ('If you are not limited by equipment space restrictions, multiple (up to four) rows of onions can be planted on raised beds covered with black plastic mulch.') is from Penn State Extension's onion-production guide, which is explicitly framed for small-scale/part-time COMMERCIAL farming operations (the surrounding section discusses 75,000-120,000 plants/acre spacing and drip-tape irrigation). It is a conditional, equipment-driven description of one commercial raised-bed configuration among several, not a general statement that onion's soil_base is 'garden_bed.' No source was actually cited establishing a general garden-bed (in-ground, non-container) growing categorization for the species; the specific quote chosen doesn't support the general field value it's attached to.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The value 'moderate' does not appear in any cited source — the quotes only say 'well-drained' (Clemson, and NC State/RHS per the record's own unknowns note). 'Well-drained' and 'moderate drainage' are not interchangeable in standard garden-drainage vocabulary (well-drained typically indicates better-than-moderate drainage), and the record itself admits in unknowns that 'no source uses the catalog's own drainage vocabulary directly' — i.e., this is the researcher's own unverified translation into the catalog's category set, asserted as a factual field value rather than left null or hedged.

records.name_note: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox gives the accepted name for garden pea as Lathyrus oleraceus, listing Pisum sativum (and several infraspecific names) as synonyms — this matches the modern taxonomic reclassification of the cultivated pea. Other admissible sources consulted (RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, UMD Extension, UGA CAES) continue to use Pisum sativum as the current name in their own materials, reflecting the older/still-common horticultural usage. scientific_name_given is recorded as given (Pisum sativum); scientific_name_accepted follows NC State's stated accepted binomial.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, UMD Extension, UGA CAES, RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden) states anything about toxicity of pea foliage, seeds, or pods to pets; left null rather than assuming a food crop is automatically pet-safe.

day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max: UMD states growth is favored by 'intermediate temperatures (65°-70°F)' and NC State states peas 'stop growing at temperatures above 85 degrees F,' but neither source splits these into day-specific vs. night-specific readings, so not force-mapped to a day or night field.

direct_sun_hours_max / light_fc_min / light_fc_good: this is an outdoor garden crop; admissible sources give sun-duration categories and hour counts (full sun, at least 6 hrs/day, prefers 8-10 hrs/day per UMD) rather than an indoor footcandle intensity or a stated harmful maximum, so left null in favor of outdoor_sun_exposure.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient air humidity requirements for this outdoor garden crop.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: Clemson gives only a one-time preplant rate (5-10-10 fertilizer at 3 lb/100 sq ft), not a recurring schedule; UMD (peas are a 'heavy user of nitrogen') and Clemson (warns against over-fertilizing with nitrogen since peas fix their own via Rhizobium) also give conflicting general nitrogen guidance, so no fertilize_* field was populated.
water_check_depth_cm: Clemson states watering should moisten soil to a depth of 6 in, but that describes irrigation depth achieved, not a pre-watering dryness-check depth, so left null.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source states a watering frequency/interval in days; peas are a fast-cycling annual with no dormant period, so there is no basis for either estimate.
cool_rest_note: not applicable — no source describes a winter dormancy/rest period for this fast-cycling annual vegetable.

soil_drainage (moderate) and soil_base (garden_bed): no source uses these exact schema category words; the values are inferred from qualitative descriptions of well-drained, moisture-retentive garden soil (NC State: 'Good Drainage'/'Moist'; Clemson: organic matter to loosen clay and retain moisture in sand) and explicit in-ground/row sowing instructions (UMD: 'Sow seed in garden'), so treat as a categorical read rather than a literal source term.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: Value 32 is sourced from the UGA CAES quote 'temperatures below 32 degrees can kill young blooms' — verified live against fieldreport.caes.uga.edu, which explicitly scopes the 32F kill point to young blooms/flowers only ('the plant will endure some cold weather' generally). The record's own Clemson citation in this same record confirms the general plant 'can withstand frosts and light freezes, although the blossoms cannot' — i.e. the whole plant tolerates temperatures at/below 32F and only the blooms are lost. Populating chill_damage_f (a whole-plant field) with a reproductive-tissue-specific kill temperature conflates 'this flower dies here' with 'this plant sustains chill damage here,' which is exactly the kind of survival-floor/scope mismatch the audit calls out. The digit itself is quoted correctly, but the field it was mapped onto over-generalizes a narrower claim.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The supporting citation's quote — 'Synonym(s): Pisum abyssinicum, Pisum arvense, Pisum sativum, Pisum sativum subsp. arvense, Pisum sativum subsp. elatius' — is not verbatim from the cited NC State page. I fetched https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/pisum-sativum/ directly (three independent checks, including an explicit search for the literal string 'Synonym'): the page's actual heading for that list is 'Previously known as:', and the word 'Synonym' does not appear anywhere on the page. The underlying substantive conclusion (page titled 'Lathyrus oleraceus,' with Pisum sativum listed as a prior name) does check out and scientific_name_accepted='Lathyrus oleraceus' is verbatim from the source's own title, so the field value itself survives — but the citation's quote text was fabricated/paraphrased rather than lifted from the source, which fails the 'does the quote actually state this' verbatim-fidelity check regardless of whether the conclusion happens to be right.
records.water_dry_down_target: Keep the root zone consistently moist; water deeply enough to moisten soil to about 6 in (15 cm) depth rather than light sprinklings, which encourage shallow rooting.

unknowns: toxic_to_pets: no admissible source directly addresses toxicity of Capsicum annuum / pepper to dogs or cats. NC State's Poison panel for the Longum Group (chili/cayenne varieties) marks 'Poison to Humans: Yes' with pain/GI/skin-irritation symptoms from capsaicin, but that panel is explicitly human-toxicity data, is on a variety-level page (not all Capsicum annuum varieties, e.g. bell peppers, are high in capsaicin), and never mentions dogs, cats, or pets. A Clemson HGIC article on spicy birdseed separately notes capsaicin 'may negatively impact your pets and cause a burning sensation' but frames this as irritant discomfort, not toxicity, and doesn't name the whole plant. Neither source supports a true/false call, so the field is left null per the harm-capable-field rule rather than inferred from human-toxicity or genus-level data.

chill_damage_f: sources (Clemson, Penn State) say not to transplant/plant until after last frost or until soil warms, but none states the specific air temperature at which cold/frost damage begins for this crop.

soil_drainage: NC State tags this species 'Good Drainage' and Clemson recommends 'well-drained, loamy, or sandy loam soil,' but neither uses language that maps cleanly onto the fast/moderate/moisture_retentive enum without guessing, so left null.

fertilize_interval_days: Clemson describes two side-dress applications spaced 'three to four weeks' apart, a range rather than a single value; left null rather than picking an arbitrary point in that range.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source discusses ambient humidity requirements for this outdoor garden crop.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: sources give only the qualitative 'full sun (6+ hours)' category for this garden crop, not footcandle intensity values or an hours-of-sun ceiling; captured instead via outdoor_sun_exposure per the field notes.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives day-interval or check-depth watering guidance for this crop; only the qualitative 'keep soil consistently and evenly moist' statement was found (captured as water_regime).
fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: no source gives specific active months or a dilution-strength (full/half/quarter) recommendation.
cool_rest_note: not applicable/no source addresses a dormancy or cool-rest period for this warm-season annual crop.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note asserts that Capsicum annuum is 'the name used consistently across every admissible source consulted (Clemson HGIC, NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, Penn State Extension)' -- but the citations array contains zero Penn State Extension (extension.psu.edu) entries anywhere in the record. No quote, URL, or claim from Penn State backs this up. The record is citing a source's corroboration that isn't actually present in its own evidence chain, which is exactly the kind of unverifiable overreach the audit is meant to catch, even though the underlying value (scientific_name_accepted = 'Capsicum annuum', matching the given name and every source that IS actually cited) checks out as correct on its own. Either drop the Penn State claim from name_note or add the missing citation.

records.name_note: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists Solanum andigenum, Solanum phureja, and Solanum subandigenum as names "previously known" for this plant; Solanum tuberosum (the name given) is the current name used consistently across every admissible source consulted, so it is also entered as the accepted name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox rates this species "High" poison severity, names solanine and other alkaloids as the toxic principle, lists fruits, leaves, roots and stems as the poisonous parts, gives possible symptoms of nausea, vomiting, salivation, drowsiness, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weakness and respiratory depression that "may be fatal," and separately flags it a problem for cats, dogs, horses and children. The same page explains that all green parts of the plant -- the sprouts, stems, leaves, berries, and the green skin of the tuber -- contain this solanine; the normal (non-green) tuber is the edible part. No admissible source gave a conflicting "non-toxic" claim for this species -- the other sources consulted simply don't address pet toxicity.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: UGA gives a watering interval ('Heavier soil needs watering at least once every 5 to 7 days, but sandy soils may need even more frequent irrigation') but it is soil-texture-dependent and given as a range, not a single species-level day count, so left null rather than picking a bound.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The citation's claim text says the RHS quote shows container potatoes 'positioned in full sun outdoors/in a greenhouse, not grown as an indoor houseplant,' but the actual quoted sentence ('Plant one seed potato in a 30cm pot, position it in full sun and keep it well watered') only says 'full sun' -- it says nothing about outdoors or a greenhouse. Those words are pulled from an unquoted, different part of the RHS page (a frost-protection passage about keeping containers in a frost-free greenhouse until risk of frost passes) and spliced into the claim as if the cited quote supported them. The underlying value (is_houseplant: false) is almost certainly correct for potatoes regardless, but the citation as written attributes to its quote more than the quote actually says.

soil_base — removed on audit: The value 'garden_bed' is backed by the same citation used for outdoor_sun_exposure/soil_drainage, whose quote ('Potatoes grow best in full sun and well-drained, sandy and acidic soil...') describes soil texture and drainage, not a growing-location category. Nothing in the quote distinguishes garden-bed cultivation from the container/pot cultivation the RHS source (also in this record's citation list) documents as a legitimate alternative method. The claim label bundles 'soil_base garden_bed' onto a quote that doesn't establish it.

records.name_note: Every admissible source consulted (NC State Extension, Clemson HGIC, Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension, RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden) refers to this species as Spinacia oleracea without indicating a synonym or a different currently-accepted binomial; scientific_name_accepted therefore matches scientific_name_given.

chill_damage_f: sources give mature-plant and seedling survival/tolerance floors (Clemson/NC State: mature plant survives to 20°F without injury; Penn State: seedlings tolerate 15°F-20°F; RHS hardiness rating H4 = -10 to -5°C) but none states the temperature at which cold/frost damage actually begins, so left null.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a footcandle figure for spinach; as an outdoor garden crop, sun exposure is described only in duration/category terms, which is captured in outdoor_sun_exposure instead.

direct_sun_hours_max: sources give differing hour figures for different purposes (NC State: plant tolerates as little as 3-4 hours of sun/day; UMD: partial shade is defined as 4-6 hours of direct light/day) with no single clean 'maximum sun tolerated' figure, so left null.

humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source discusses ambient growing humidity for spinach (UMD mentions 95% RH but only as a post-harvest cold-storage condition, not a growing requirement).

water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target: water_regime is keep_moist rather than a dry-down regime; Clemson's instruction to 'moisten the soil to a depth of 6 inches' describes irrigation thoroughness, not a moisture-check depth used to decide when to water, so it was not mapped to these fields.

water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no source gives a specific watering-frequency interval in days, only qualitative language ('consistent supply of moisture', 'water deeply and regularly'), so left null rather than inventing a schedule.

fertilize_interval_days: Clemson describes a single side-dress application of calcium nitrate timed three to four weeks after planting (possibly split into two applications on sandy soil), which is not a repeating fertilization interval, so left null.
fertilize_strength / fertilize_active_months: no admissible source gives fertilizer dilution/strength guidance or specific calendar months for fertilizing.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source discusses a dormancy or winter-rest period for this annual crop; not applicable/found.

soil_base — removed on audit: The record sets soil_base='garden_bed' and cites Clemson HGIC's 'Spinach grows well on a variety of soils, but it prefers a fertile sandy loam high in organic matter' as support. That quote is about soil texture/fertility only — it never addresses bed vs. container cultivation, so it does not actually establish 'garden_bed' as opposed to any other soil_base bucket. Worse, the record's own separate NC State citation ('It can be grown at home in containers or beds') directly documents container cultivation as an equally valid, non-exclusive setting, which is confirmed by NC State's page text stating spinach 'can be grown in containers as small as 1 gallon and as shallow as 4 to 6 inches.' This same catalog has an established, audited precedent for exactly this situation: when admissible sources document both in-ground/garden-bed cultivation and container cultivation as separate, non-exclusive settings, soil_base is left null rather than picking one bucket, specifically 'to avoid overstating one setting as the only one' (see garden-gnome/app/data/verified/b10-veg-round3.json, Cucumber and Eggplant records). The Spinach record breaks with that precedent, picking 'garden_bed' exclusively on a citation that doesn't even speak to the question, while its own other citation shows containers are equally valid.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering frequency in days or a pre-watering moisture-check depth; Clemson states a depth to moisten the soil TO when watering (6 inches), which is a different measurement and was not mapped onto water_check_depth_cm.

soil_base: RHS notes compact summer-squash varieties can also be grown in large containers of multi-purpose or soil-based compost, but the field holds one value; recorded as garden_bed because RHS calls in-ground growing the usual method ('Squashes are usually grown in the ground... but compact varieties of summer squash can be grown in large containers').

soil_ph: Clemson's winter squash/pumpkin factsheet gives a slightly different pH window (6.2-6.5) than its summer squash factsheet (6.0-6.5) used here, and NC State's general species tag is broader ('Neutral (6.0-8.0)'); the summer squash figures were used as the recorded value since they are the most specific numeric statement found.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The only source for this number is RHS: 'Apply an organic-based, high potassium liquid fertiliser every 10 to 14 days once the first fruits start to swell' — and RHS explicitly qualifies this to container-grown plants only, immediately preceded by 'Squashes growing in the ground shouldn't need feeding.' The record's own soil_base field is 'garden_bed' (RHS: 'usually grown in the ground'), i.e. the record has already picked in-ground as the representative growing method — yet fertilize_interval_days=14 is populated as a general, unqualified field for that same record, which per the very same source needs NO feeding at all. A downstream consumer reading soil_base=garden_bed + fertilize_interval_days=14 would tell an in-ground grower to fertilize every 14 days, directly contradicting the cited source's guidance for that exact scenario. The 14-day figure is real (drawn from a genuine 10-14 day range) but its applicability condition (container-grown, post-fruit-set only) was dropped from the general field instead of being reflected as a caveat or left null/conditional.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The cited RHS quote ('Squashes are usually grown in the ground... but compact varieties of summer squash can be grown in large containers') distinguishes ground vs. container growing — it says nothing about indoor vs. outdoor placement, so it does not literally state 'not a houseplant.' The conclusion is very likely correct in reality (squash needs 6+ hours direct sun, per the record's own full_sun citations, which is a far more direct basis for ruling out houseplant status), but the specific quote chosen for this claim only sounds related to the field rather than actually asserting it. The record should have cited the full-sun/outdoor-siting language (e.g. RHS's 'Choose a warm growing site in full sun') rather than the ground-vs-container sentence, which addresses a different axis (location type, not indoor/outdoor).

records.name_note: RHS profiles this taxon as "Brassica rapa Rapifera Group" with a page field reading "Name Status" / "Accepted", and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder likewise catalogs turnip as "Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group)". Neither of these, nor Clemson HGIC or UGA CAES, ever uses the infraspecific label "subsp. rapa" given in the research brief — all admissible sources that go below the species level use the horticultural "Rapifera Group" designation instead. scientific_name_accepted is therefore set to Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group), the form an admissible source explicitly marks as accepted, rather than to a "subsp. rapa" form no source confirms or to a spliced combination of the two.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a specific damage-onset temperature for turnip; UGA CAES states only that 'hard frosts can kill the crops or make them unmarketable' (no number), and UMD's 15-20°F figure is a survival-tolerance floor for turnip greens (grouped with kale as 'the latter two') rather than a damage-onset value, so neither was used.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: UGA CAES Table 2 gives a turnip-specific 'Optimum Air Temperature for Crop Growth (°F): 60-65' but does not split it into day vs. night readings, so it was not mapped onto either field.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: none of the admissible sources (Clemson HGIC, RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, UGA CAES, UMD Extension) discuss toxicity to pets, dogs, cats, or livestock for turnip; all describe it strictly as a human food crop (root and greens).

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source states an ambient air-humidity requirement for turnip; it is an outdoor garden crop and the extension sources discuss soil moisture, not air humidity.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources describe sun exposure only in category terms (full sun/partial shade), never as footcandles or an hours-of-direct-light count for turnip specifically.

soil_drainage: sources describe the soil qualitatively as 'well-drained' (Clemson, MOBOT) or 'moist but well-drained' (RHS) but never in fast/moderate/moisture_retentive terms, so no enum tier was guessed.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: Clemson describes a single side-dress of calcium nitrate three to four weeks after planting (split into two applications three to four weeks apart only on sandy soil) — a one-time, growth-stage-timed application, not a recurring feeding interval or a houseplant-style dilution strength, so it was not mapped to these fields.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering frequency in days or a soil-check depth for turnip; only qualitative moisture guidance ('keep soil evenly moist', 'water in dry weather') was found.
water_dry_down_target: not populated; the sourced regime is continuous even moisture rather than a stated dry-down point between waterings, and no source frames it that way.
cool_rest_note: not applicable / no admissible source describes a dormancy or cool-rest period for turnip distinct from its normal cool-season growing window.

soil_ph: RHS classifies turnip's pH preference only in the broad category 'Alkaline or Neutral', which does not fully align with Clemson's specific 6.0–6.5 target range; this reads as a difference in precision (categorical vs. numeric) rather than a stated factual conflict, so Clemson's specific figure was used and RHS's categorical note is flagged here for transparency.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The citation backing this field quotes RHS's page field 'Name Status: Accepted', but RHS's own page writes the taxon without parentheses ('Brassica rapa Rapifera Group') -- confirmed via both AI extraction and raw HTML title of https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/157219/brassica-rapa-rapifera-group/details. The actual value placed in the field, 'Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group)' with parentheses, is not literally present in that quote -- it matches MOBOT's exact formatting instead (verified verbatim in MOBOT's raw HTML: 'Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group) ... Common Name: turnip'). MOBOT is cited elsewhere in the record (common_name, water_regime) but never cited for the scientific-name claim itself, so the citation attached to scientific_name_accepted does not actually support the specific string it's labeled as backing -- a quote/claim mismatch even though the value is independently verifiable from a different source in the record.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: two loader-found defects fixed before landing, both the same class as b8's Artichoke -- Garden Pea and Turnip each had a citation and name_note that already established a specific accepted name (Lathyrus oleraceus, cited to NC State's synonymy listing; Brassica rapa (Rapifera Group), cited to RHS's own 'Name Status: Accepted' field) but left scientific_name_accepted null despite the prompt explicitly warning against this after b8. Populated from evidence already in each record, not invented. Neither left the record without a usable subject -- claims_from_record falls back to scientific_name_given -- but both are now correctly named.

The batch's more important result is a negative one: the conflict- resolution fix added after b10 (a genuine cross-source disagreement on a harm-capable field must be nulled, not decided by preference) held across the whole batch. Onion's water_regime resolved to null with Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Dry to medium' rating explicitly left in conflict against Clemson and UMD's 'ample moisture during bulb enlargement' -- exactly the shape of the Cucumber defect from b10, this time handled correctly at the source. Potato's toxicity call is solid and correctly separates the edible tuber from the genuinely toxic green parts (solanine).
